notable_claims: Principles of academic freedom should apply to academic computer systems.
Personal files in university home directories should have the same privacy protections as physical office or dorm spaces.
Suspension from a computer is a serious penalty requiring due process similar to formal disciplinary warnings.
The selection of newsgroups on academic sites should follow library standards for selecting books and magazines.
classification.summary: Carl M. Kadie presents a draft framework intended to codify the application of academic freedom principles to university computer systems. The document organizes these as 'principles' (axioms) and 'interpretations' (theorems), drawing heavily from existing library standards and student rights statements. It addresses key areas including due process for account suspension, privacy of home directories, and the prevention of censorship in digital publications.
classification.title: Draft Statement on Computers and Academic Freedom (CAF)

identity.subject: Draft Statement on Computers and Academic Freedom (CAF)

notable_claims: The EFF maintained a public archive specifically dedicated to collecting and critiquing university computer policies.
classification.summary: This document serves as a directory for the Computer Policy and Critiques Archive, hosted by the Electronic Freedom Foundation (EFF). The archive collected computer use policies from various academic institutions and included corresponding critiques of those policies. It provided access via anonymous FTP and email to facilitate the study of institutional computing restrictions.
classification.title: README file for Computer Policy and Critiques Archive

identity.subject: README file for Computer Policy and Critiques Archive

notable_claims: Using university resources to publish pornography in a forum where it can be seen as sexual harassment is not protected freedom of speech.
classification.summary: Barry Grau, Interim Manager of User Services at the University of Illinois - Chicago, apologizes for a specific inappropriate post and details disciplinary actions taken against the author. He argues that while freedom of speech is supported, using university resources to publish pornography in forums where it constitutes sexual harassment is not protected speech.

notable_claims: University newsgroup facilities function as 'limited public forums' under the Public-Forum Doctrine.
Content-based prohibitions in limited public forums must be narrowly drawn to effectuate a compelling state interest.
Statements in free-speech forums like soc.women should not be classified as sexual harassment to justify censorship.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie challenges a university administrator's decision to punish a student for posting content deemed pornographic or harassing. Kadie argues that university newsgroup facilities constitute 'limited public forums' and that the punishment violates both campus codes of conduct and First Amendment rights. The post emphasizes that using university resources for expression should not be subject to institutional censorship.
classification.title: Re: yahweh is good posting

notable_claims: Courts have treated sysadmins as either postmasters (private mail) or publishers (publications).
Sysops of private BBSs have been successfully sued and possess the right to control content.
The legality of pulling university accounts without due process remains undetermined without a legal test case.
classification.summary: Amy Gorin discusses the legal liabilities of system administrators regarding content moderation on Usenet and BBSs. She argues that sysadmins may be viewed as either postmasters or publishers under existing law and suggests that a test case is necessary to determine the legality of account termination without due process in university settings.

notable_claims: Sysops of private BBSs have been successfully sued and can control content.
University policies on the free exchange of ideas create a different legal standing than private BBSs.
Netnews occupies a legal gray area between private email and formal publication.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding the legal liability of system administrators and the nature of Usenet as a medium. The participants debate whether newsgroups should be treated as private mail or publications, and whether university policies on free exchange of ideas protect offensive content from censorship.

notable_claims: University administrators labeling or restricting posts based on newsgroup appropriateness is a form of censorship.
Unmoderated Usenet and Altnet groups should be treated as free-speech forums where charters define focus rather than legal boundaries.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie responds to Aydin Edguer regarding whether university system administrators should punish users for posting off-topic content. While Edguer argues that violating the social contract of a forum's scope warrants consequences, Kadie contends that unmoderated newsgroups are free-speech forums. Kadie asserts that official university intervention in directing posts constitutes censorship and that only social disapproval is appropriate.
classification.title: Official punishment of off-topic posts

notable_claims: Off-topic posts that can be filtered by kill files likely do not meet the threshold for 'substantial interference with the rights of others'.
University disciplinary processes are required before penalties for disruptive action can be imposed.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie discusses the application of University of Illinois conduct rules to online behavior and censorship. He argues that off-topic posts do not constitute 'substantial interference with the rights of others' if they can be managed via kill files. The post includes a detailed excerpt of university regulations regarding disruptive or coercive action.

notable_claims: Online disclaimers may reduce the 'outraged user' syndrome from an administrator's perspective.
Users should be held personally responsible for law-violating posts rather than the hosting site.
classification.summary: Wes Morgan proposes the use of an online disclaimer displayed upon accessing Usenet software as an alternative to physical 'news contracts.' The goal was to clarify that users, not the institution or site administrator, are responsible for the content they read and post. This reflects early administrative efforts to manage legal and ethical liability associated with decentralized network communication.
classification.title: Online disclaimers?

notable_claims: One of the first cases of high-tech harassment involving electronic mail.
Court ordered a party to stay away from an individual and organization both physically and electronically.
classification.summary: A report on a legal ruling in Seattle where a judge issued a restraining order against a former Microsoft employee. The court ordered Joan Brewer to cease both physical and electronic contact with Bill Gates and Microsoft following a series of unwelcome emails.
classification.title: Harassment via Email

notable_claims: The alt.sex.* hierarchy was removed from PSUVM
Official reason for removal was cost-cutting
Potential reason for removal was the content of specific postings
classification.summary: Gregory G. Nagy reports that the alt.sex.* newsgroup hierarchy was removed from Penn State's main general purpose computer, PSUVM. While administration cited cost-cutting as the reason, Nagy suggests it may have been due to specific controversial postings originating from the machine.
classification.title: Removal of alt.sex.* hierarchy on PSUVM

notable_claims: University computing policies should be consistent with the institution's general search and seizure procedures for physical spaces.
Suspending computing privileges during an investigation may contradict the principle of 'innocent until found guilty' and existing university codes.
Broad contradictions exist in policies that prohibit all personal use while explicitly permitting game playing.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie of the EFF critiques UCLA's SEASnet computing policies, arguing that they lack clarity regarding noncommercial personal use and violate student privacy. He advocates for aligning computer search and suspension procedures with the university's general academic freedom and student rights standards. The post emphasizes the need for broad community participation in developing computing policies.
classification.title: Re: Ucla's Use Policies
